name: Australia
region: Australia and New Zealand itinerary region
cruiseCalls: Brisbane, Broome, Cairns, Darwin, Perth (Fremantle), Sydney, Willis Island (scenic cruising)
atAGlance: Population about 27.6 million; area 7,688,287 km²; nominal GDP around US$1.8 trillion; capital Canberra; English is predominant, alongside hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages; currency Australian dollar (AUD). An island continent with no land borders; nearby neighbours include Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and New Zealand.
government: Australia is a federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with six states and two mainland territories. Institutions are stable, elections competitive and the judiciary independent. The 2025 federal election returned the Australian Labor Party under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with a majority in the House of Representatives. Debates include housing affordability, Indigenous reconciliation, migration, energy transition, cost of living and the balance between mining and climate commitments. Australia is a close US ally and an important Indo-Pacific power.
economy: Mining (iron ore, coal, natural gas, lithium and other minerals), agriculture, education, healthcare, financial services, tourism, construction, retail and professional services are important. Natural-resource exports connect Australia closely to Asian markets. Services employ most workers, but resource exports have an outsized role in trade and government revenue. Regional economies are specialised and distances are vast.
timeline: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have maintained societies, languages, trade networks and cultural traditions on the continent for at least 65,000 years. James Cook charted the east coast for Britain in 1770; the First Fleet arrived in 1788 and began British colonisation at Sydney Cove. The six colonies federated in 1901. Darwin was bombed by Japan in 1942. The 1967 referendum enabled the Commonwealth to make laws for Aboriginal people and include them in population counts; struggles for rights and recognition continued. The prime minister apologised to the Stolen Generations in 2008; a referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament was defeated in 2023.
people: Cathy Freeman (Olympic runner); Banjo Paterson and Miles Franklin (writers); Tim Winton (writer); Cate Blanchett and Hugh Jackman (actors); AC/DC (rock band); David Unaipon (Aboriginal inventor and writer).
culture: Australia occupies an entire continent, with ecosystems ranging from tropical rainforest to desert, alpine country and temperate forest. The Great Barrier Reef is the world's largest coral reef system; Cairns is a gateway to reef and rainforest. Broome is associated with pearling and the Kimberley; Darwin has strong Southeast Asian connections and was rebuilt after Cyclone Tracy in 1974. Willis Island is a small, remote coral cay in the Coral Sea, best known for its weather-monitoring station; scenic cruising means viewing it from the ship rather than a normal landing. Indigenous Australian cultures are among the world's oldest continuing cultural traditions, with remarkable diversity among language groups and regions.

name: Belgium
atAGlance: Population about 11.9 million; area 30,528 km²; nominal GDP around US$725 billion; capital Brussels; official languages Dutch, French and German; currency euro (EUR). Borders France, Luxembourg, Germany and the Netherlands; the North Sea coastline is short but economically important.
government: Belgium is a federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy. Powers are divided among federal, regional and community governments, and coalitions often require agreements across language communities. In November 2026 the governing coalition faced a high-profile budget standoff. King Philippe rejected Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s resignation and directed the five-party coalition to resume negotiations, with a report-back deadline of 16 November and a 31 December deadline for the 2027 budget. This is political bargaining within established institutions, not a breakdown of the state. [Associated Press, 6 November 2026](https://apnews.com/article/6ef749a5875cb78e486480d28506a7a3).
economy: Belgium is a developed, trade-oriented economy with important chemicals, pharmaceuticals, food processing, machinery, logistics, finance, diamond trading and professional services. The Port of Antwerp-Bruges is one of Europe's major maritime gateways. Brussels hosts key EU and NATO institutions, creating a major international-services sector. Public debt and the federal budget are recurring policy challenges.
timeline: The 1830 revolution led to independence from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands; Leopold I became king in 1831. King Leopold II's control of the Congo Free State (1885–1908) was marked by severe atrocities, leading to Belgian state annexation in 1908. Germany invaded Belgium in both World Wars. Belgium was a founding member of the European Economic Community in 1957. Constitutional reforms from the 1970s to 1993 transformed it into a federal state.
people: Adolphe Sax (inventor of the saxophone); René Magritte (surrealist artist); Hergé (creator of Tintin); Audrey Hepburn (actor, born in Brussels); Stromae (musician); Georges Lemaître (physicist associated with the Big Bang theory).
culture: Belgium has three official languages and distinct Dutch-speaking Flemish, French-speaking Walloon and German-speaking communities. It is renowned for chocolate, waffles, beer and fries; its beer culture includes hundreds of styles and abbey and Trappist traditions. Bruges's medieval centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site, with canals, merchant houses and market squares. Comic art is a major cultural export: Tintin, the Smurfs and Lucky Luke are Belgian creations.

name: The Bahamas
cruiseCalls: Celebration Key (Grand Bahama), Freeport (Grand Bahama), Nassau (New Providence)
atAGlance: Population about 403,000; land area about 13,880 km² across a large archipelago; nominal GDP roughly US$15–16 billion (latest comparable value may lag the current year); capital Nassau; language English; currency Bahamian dollar (BSD), pegged one-to-one with the US dollar. The Bahamas lie southeast of Florida, northeast of Cuba and northwest of Turks and Caicos.
government: The Bahamas is a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy. Prime Minister Philip Davis and the Progressive Liberal Party won re-election in the 12 May 2026 general election. Institutions are well established for the region. Policy challenges include violent crime, housing affordability, public debt, hurricane exposure, inequality and the economy's heavy reliance on tourism.
economy: Tourism dominates employment and foreign exchange, especially resorts, cruise tourism, hotels, boating and related services. International financial services, construction, real estate, fishing and maritime activity supplement the sector. Dependence on imported food and energy and vulnerability to tropical storms are major structural risks.
timeline: Lucayan Taíno people inhabited the islands before European contact. Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas in the Bahamian archipelago in 1492, at an island traditionally identified as San Salvador/Guanahani. The islands became a British Crown Colony in 1718; Nassau acquired a pirate-haven reputation. Slavery was abolished in the British Empire in 1834. The Bahamas became independent on 10 July 1973 and remained in the Commonwealth.
people: Sidney Poitier was born in Miami to Bahamian parents and grew up in the Bahamas; he became an internationally celebrated actor and director. Shaunae Miller-Uibo (Olympic sprinter) and Mychal Thompson (basketball, born in Nassau) are prominent sporting figures. Cultural scholar and writer Nicolette Bethel is an important voice in Bahamian public life.
culture: There are more than 700 islands and cays, though only a few dozen are inhabited. Junkanoo is a spectacular festival of costumes, drums, cowbells and dance, especially around Christmas and New Year. Conch is a culinary staple, served in fritters, salad and chowder. Grand Bahama has pine forests, wetlands, caves and mangroves as well as beaches and resort areas. Celebration Key and Freeport are both on Grand Bahama, while Nassau is on New Providence.

name: Belize
atAGlance: Population about 423,000; area 22,966 km²; nominal GDP about US$3.3 billion; capital Belmopan (largest city: Belize City); official language English; currency Belize dollar (BZD), fixed at BZ$2 to US$1. Neighbours are Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south; the Caribbean Sea lies to the east.
government: Belize is a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, with a governor-general representing the monarch. It has competitive elections and a relatively open civic environment. The country operates on a small-state scale, so government capacity, public finances and infrastructure are constrained. A long-running territorial claim by Guatemala remains a diplomatic and legal issue; the dispute was referred to the International Court of Justice by agreement in 2019.
economy: Tourism, agriculture and fisheries are central. Sugar, citrus, bananas, marine products and small-scale manufacturing contribute, alongside offshore services and a modest petroleum sector. The small economy is exposed to hurricanes, global food and fuel prices and changes in visitor arrivals. Maya heritage, the barrier reef and nature tourism are major assets.
timeline: The region formed part of the Maya world, with major centres such as Caracol, Lamanai and Xunantunich. British logwood and mahogany cutters established a presence in the 17th and 18th centuries; the settlement became British Honduras and a Crown Colony in 1862. Belize became independent on 21 September 1981. Guatemala recognised independence in 1992 while maintaining a territorial claim.
people: George Price (independence leader and first prime minister); Andy Palacio (musician and Garifuna cultural advocate); Philip Goldson (political figure); Belize-born athlete Marion Jones later competed for the United States.
culture: Belize is the only Central American country whose official language is English. The Belize Barrier Reef is part of the Mesoamerican Reef system, the world's second-largest reef system after Australia's Great Barrier Reef. The Great Blue Hole is a striking marine sinkhole. Garifuna culture blends West/Central African and Indigenous Caribbean heritage; punta music, dance and food are important cultural expressions. Try rice and beans, stew chicken, fry jacks and conch.

name: Germany
atAGlance: Population about 83.5 million; area 357,588 km²; nominal GDP around US$5.0 trillion; capital Berlin; language German, with Danish, Sorbian, Frisian and Romani recognised minority languages; currency euro (EUR). Borders Denmark, Poland, Czechia, Austria, Switzerland, France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands; the Baltic and North seas provide maritime access.
government: Germany is a federal parliamentary republic with 16 federal states. It has robust democratic institutions and an independent judiciary. Political debate is shaped by coalition negotiations, migration, energy prices, industrial competitiveness, fiscal rules, the rise of anti-establishment parties and support for Ukraine. The post-war constitutional order places strong protections around democratic institutions. Warnemünde is on the Baltic coast, some distance from Berlin; cruise excursions to the capital involve a substantial journey.
economy: Germany is Europe's largest economy and a major global exporter. Key sectors include automotive manufacturing, machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, electrical equipment, software, logistics, finance and renewable energy. The Mittelstand—often family-owned, highly specialised medium-sized firms—is distinctive. Challenges include an ageing workforce, energy transition costs, infrastructure renewal and global manufacturing competition.
timeline: The German Empire unified in 1871 under Prussian leadership. Defeat in World War I led to the abdication of the Kaiser and the Weimar Republic. The Nazi dictatorship (1933–1945) led to World War II and the Holocaust. Germany was divided into the Federal Republic in the west and the German Democratic Republic in the east after 1945. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and reunification followed on 3 October 1990. Germany became a central actor in EU integration.
people: Johann Sebastian Bach, Ludwig van Beethoven and Richard Wagner (composers); Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (writer); Albert Einstein (physicist); Hannah Arendt (political thinker); Marlene Dietrich (actor); Angela Merkel (former chancellor).
culture: Germany has 16 federal states, each with its own traditions and food. Christmas markets, regional breads, beer traditions and seasonal festivals are important. The Autobahn has sections without a general speed limit, but many stretches have limits and an advisory speed applies elsewhere. Berlin's 20th-century history is unusually visible: the city was divided by the Wall from 1961 to 1989. Germany's cultural influence includes classical music, philosophy, literature, design and cinema as well as engineering.

name: Denmark
atAGlance: Population about 6 million; area 42,933 km² for metropolitan Denmark; the Kingdom also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands; nominal GDP around US$460 billion; capital Copenhagen; language Danish (Faroese and Greenlandic are official in their self-governing territories); currency Danish krone (DKK). Metropolitan Denmark borders Germany and is connected to Sweden by bridges and ferries.
government: Denmark is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy. Greenland and the Faroe Islands have extensive self-government. Policy focuses on welfare services, climate and energy, immigration, defence and the future of the Danish Realm. Greenlandic self-government and Arctic security are increasingly prominent. Denmark is an EU and NATO member but retains EU opt-outs in some policy areas.
economy: Pharmaceuticals and life sciences, shipping, food processing, agriculture, wind energy, design, machinery and professional services are major sectors. Maersk is a global shipping group with Danish origins; Danish companies are prominent in medical technology and renewable energy. The economy is highly open to trade and benefits from strong institutions and infrastructure.
timeline: Danish Viking networks traded, raided and settled across northern Europe and the North Atlantic. The Kalmar Union (1397) brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch. The Reformation established Lutheranism in 1536. Denmark adopted a constitution in 1849 and moved away from absolute monarchy. Nazi Germany occupied Denmark during World War II. Denmark joined the European Economic Community in 1973; Greenland obtained home rule in 1979 and expanded self-government in 2009.
people: Hans Christian Andersen (fairy-tale writer); Niels Bohr (physicist); Karen Blixen (writer); Søren Kierkegaard (philosopher); Mads Mikkelsen (actor); Lars von Trier (film-maker).
culture: Hygge describes cosy togetherness and everyday comfort. LEGO began in Billund; the name comes from leg godt, “play well.” Danish pastries are known locally as wienerbrød (“Viennese bread”). Copenhagen's cycling infrastructure is part of everyday life. The Danish Realm makes Denmark an Arctic country as well as a Baltic and North Sea country, because of Greenland and the Faroe Islands.

name: Dominican Republic
atAGlance: Population about 11.5 million; area 48,671 km²; nominal GDP roughly US$125–130 billion; capital Santo Domingo; language Spanish; currency Dominican peso (DOP). It shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti and sits between Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Greater Antilles.
government: The Dominican Republic is a presidential republic with competitive multiparty elections. President Luis Abinader won re-election in 2024, and the next regular presidential election is expected in 2028. Institutions are comparatively established in the Caribbean, but corruption, public-service quality, inequality, crime, migration and the difficult relationship with Haiti remain major political issues. The country is not politically uniform: the capital, tourist corridors, border provinces and rural areas have different economic and social experiences.
economy: Tourism is a major foreign-exchange earner, alongside manufacturing in free-trade zones, mining (notably gold and nickel), agriculture, retail and financial services. Remittances from the Dominican diaspora are important to household income. It is one of the more diversified large economies in the Caribbean, but growth and public services are uneven between regions.
timeline: Taíno communities inhabited Hispaniola before Columbus reached the island in 1492. Spain ceded the western part of the island to France in 1697, helping establish the island's later division. A short-lived independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Haitian rule; Dominican independence was proclaimed on 27 February 1844. Rafael Trujillo's dictatorship (1930–1961) left a deep legacy of repression. Civil conflict and foreign intervention followed in 1965, before a gradual return to competitive electoral politics.
people: Juan Luis Guerra (merengue and bachata); Oscar de la Renta (fashion designer, born in Santo Domingo); Junot Díaz (Pulitzer Prize-winning writer); David Ortiz and Sammy Sosa (baseball). Baseball is a central part of modern Dominican popular culture.
culture: Merengue and bachata are signature musical forms with global followings. The country contains Pico Duarte, the Caribbean's highest mountain, and Lake Enriquillo, a salt lake below sea level. Try la bandera (rice, beans and stewed meat), sancocho, fried plantains and tropical fruit. Amber Cove is a cruise development near Puerto Plata, a city with a long Atlantic trading and maritime history.

name: Estonia
atAGlance: Population about 1.37 million; area 45,339 km²; nominal GDP around US$47 billion; capital Tallinn; language Estonian (Russian is also widely spoken in some communities); currency euro (EUR). Borders Latvia to the south and Russia to the east; Finland lies across the Gulf of Finland and Sweden across the Baltic Sea.
government: Estonia is a stable parliamentary democracy and EU and NATO member. National security, cyber resilience, relations with Russia, energy independence and the integration of Russian-speaking communities are major policy concerns. Its digital-government model is internationally recognised, but cyber security and defence are central because of its position on NATO's eastern flank.
economy: IT and digital services, telecommunications, logistics, wood products, machinery, food processing, energy and professional services are important. Estonia's small population and digital infrastructure support start-ups and cross-border services. The economy is exposed to European demand and regional security and trade conditions.
timeline: Tallinn, then known as Reval, became a major Hanseatic trading city in the medieval period. Estonia declared independence in 1918. It experienced Soviet occupation, Nazi occupation during World War II and renewed Soviet rule from 1944. The Singing Revolution and mass civic mobilisation helped restore independence in 1991. Estonia joined the EU and NATO in 2004.
people: Arvo Pärt (composer); Jaan Kross (writer); Lennart Meri (writer and president); Kersti Kaljulaid (former president); Ott Tänak (rally driver).
culture: The Song Festival brings together huge choirs and is central to national identity; song gatherings helped sustain the independence movement. Estonia is a highly digitally connected state, with online public services and an e-residency programme for non-residents. Tallinn's medieval Old Town is a UNESCO site. Estonian is a Finnic language related to Finnish rather than Latvian or Lithuanian.

name: Spain
cruiseCalls: Barcelona, Cartagena, Palma de Mallorca, A Coruña, Bilbao, Cádiz, Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Vigo
atAGlance: Population about 49.4 million; area 505,990 km² (including Balearic and Canary Islands); nominal GDP around US$1.9 trillion; capital Madrid; language Spanish, with Catalan/Valencian, Galician and Basque co-official in their regions; currency euro (EUR). Spain borders Portugal, France and Andorra, and has land borders with Gibraltar and Morocco through the North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.
government: Spain is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy with 17 autonomous communities and two autonomous cities. It is a consolidated democracy and an EU and NATO member. Coalition negotiations, territorial debates (especially Catalonia), housing, migration and regional distribution of powers are recurring issues. Its regions have substantial cultural and administrative identities, so national institutions do not tell the whole story.
economy: Services dominate, particularly tourism, retail, finance, transport, health, education and professional services. Automotive production, food and beverage, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy and agriculture are also important. Spain is a major producer of olive oil, wine and citrus. Tourism is economically powerful but brings debate about housing, seasonal employment, water use and pressure on historic centres.
timeline: Rome conquered much of Iberia around the 2nd century BCE, leaving deep linguistic and infrastructural legacies. Muslim armies entered in 711; Al-Andalus became a centre of learning, architecture and trade. The Catholic Monarchs captured Granada in 1492, while Columbus's first Atlantic voyage began the Spanish overseas empire. The Peninsular War (1808–1814) and Spanish American independence movements reshaped the empire. The Spanish Civil War (1936–1939) ended with Franco's dictatorship. After Franco's death in 1975, Spain transitioned to democracy, adopted its constitution in 1978 and joined the European Communities in 1986.
people: Miguel de Cervantes (writer); Antoni Gaudí, Pablo Picasso and Salvador Dalí (artists); Penélope Cruz (actor); Rafael Nadal (tennis); Federico García Lorca (poet and playwright).
culture: Spain has 17 autonomous communities, each with its own food, festivals and sometimes languages. Barcelona's identity is strongly linked to Catalan culture; the Sagrada Família has been under construction since 1882. Flamenco is especially associated with Andalusia, not with every region equally. Try Basque pintxos, Galician seafood, Valencian paella and tapas traditions across many cities. The Canary Islands are closer to Africa than mainland Spain and have volcanic landscapes and a subtropical climate.

name: Finland
atAGlance: Population about 5.65 million; area 338,455 km²; nominal GDP around US$317 billion; capital Helsinki; official languages Finnish and Swedish, with Sámi languages protected in the north; currency euro (EUR). Borders Sweden, Norway and Russia; the Gulf of Finland separates it from Estonia.
government: Finland is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president and a prime minister responsible to parliament. It has strong democratic institutions and high public trust. Since joining NATO in 2023, security policy has been reshaped by Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the changing Baltic and Arctic security environment. Domestic debates include public debt, employment, regional services and the future of the welfare state. Finland is an EU and euro-area member.
economy: Forestry, paper and pulp, machinery, metals, electronics, telecommunications, software, clean technology, education and services are important. Finland has a strong engineering and design tradition and an export-oriented industrial base. An ageing population and regional differences are long-term economic challenges.
timeline: Finland was part of the Swedish realm for centuries. Sweden ceded Finland to Russia in 1809, and it became an autonomous Grand Duchy. Finland declared independence in 1917. The Winter War followed a Soviet invasion in 1939; Finland retained independence but ceded territory. Finland fought the Continuation War against the Soviet Union from 1941 to 1944, then joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2023.
people: Jean Sibelius (composer); Tove Jansson (creator of the Moomins); Alvar Aalto (architect and designer); Linus Torvalds (creator of the Linux kernel); Kimi Räikkönen (Formula One driver); Aki Kaurismäki (film-maker).
culture: Sauna culture is so widespread that Finland has millions of saunas for a population of around 5.6 million. The country has tens of thousands of lakes and extensive forests. The Moomins are a beloved Finnish cultural export. Helsinki's architecture blends Nordic modernism and neoclassicism. In northern Finland, summer brings midnight sun; winter brings long darkness and aurora opportunities.

name: France
atAGlance: Population about 68.7 million in metropolitan and overseas regions; area 551,695 km² metropolitan, about 643,800 km² including overseas regions and territories; nominal GDP around US$3.3–3.4 trillion; capital Paris; language French, with Breton, Occitan, Corsican and other regional languages; currency euro (EUR). Metropolitan France borders Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Monaco, Spain and Andorra; overseas France adds maritime neighbours around the world.
government: France is a semi-presidential republic with a directly elected president and a prime minister whose government must retain parliamentary support. A fragmented parliament since the 2024 snap election has made coalition-building and budgets difficult. Debates about pensions, public spending, immigration, secularism, labour reform and the role of the state are prominent. The institutions remain those of a well-established constitutional democracy, though political instability at the cabinet level is more visible than in some neighbours.
economy: Services dominate, but France has globally important aerospace, defence, luxury goods, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, food processing, transport, energy and tourism sectors. Nuclear power is central to electricity generation. French firms are major players in aircraft, trains, cosmetics, fashion and food. Public debt and fiscal adjustment are major policy challenges.
timeline: Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul in the 1st century BCE brought most of what is now France under Roman rule. The Treaty of Verdun (843) divided Charlemagne's empire and created a western kingdom that became a foundation for France. The French Revolution began in 1789 and transformed ideas about citizenship and popular sovereignty. Napoleon reshaped French institutions and fought wars across Europe. France was occupied during World War II; the Fifth Republic was founded in 1958 under Charles de Gaulle.
people: Victor Hugo (writer); Marie Curie (scientist, born in Warsaw and later a French citizen); Claude Monet (artist); Coco Chanel (fashion designer); Édith Piaf (singer); Kylian Mbappé (football).
culture: France spans several time zones because of overseas regions in the Caribbean, Indian Ocean and Pacific. Cheese and wine traditions differ from Normandy to Provence, Burgundy, Brittany, Alsace and the south-west. The national motto is Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité; 14 July commemorates the French Revolution. Marseille has long been a Mediterranean crossroads with Greek, Roman, North African and modern immigrant influences. Bordeaux is known for wine but is also a major architectural and cultural centre.

name: United Kingdom
atAGlance: Population about 69.5 million; area 243,610 km²; nominal GDP around US$4.0 trillion; capital London; language English, with Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, Scots, Irish and Ulster Scots having varying forms of recognition and use; currency pound sterling (GBP). Shares a land border with Ireland; separated from continental Europe by the English Channel and North Sea.
government: The UK is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved legislatures. The union is stable but politically contested, with constitutional debate around devolution and independence. Policy questions include public-service funding, housing, migration, regional inequality and the consequences of Brexit. The UK is not an EU member but remains in NATO and the Commonwealth.
economy: Services dominate, especially finance, insurance, professional services, technology, healthcare, education and creative industries. Aerospace, pharmaceuticals, advanced manufacturing, energy, offshore wind, oil and gas, agriculture and tourism remain important. London is a global financial centre, while the UK's regions have distinct strengths, from Scottish energy and whisky to manufacturing in northern England and industry in Wales.
timeline: Roman forces conquered much of Britain from 43 CE. The Norman Conquest of 1066 transformed monarchy, law and language. Magna Carta (1215) became an enduring symbol in constitutional history. The Acts of Union joined England and Scotland in 1707 and created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in 1801. The Industrial Revolution began in Britain and transformed manufacturing and urban life. The UK joined the European Communities in 1973 and left the EU in 2020.
people: William Shakespeare (playwright); Isaac Newton and Ada Lovelace (science and mathematics); Charles Darwin (naturalist); The Beatles (music); David Attenborough (natural-history broadcaster); J.K. Rowling (writer).
culture: The UK is a union of four nations with their own symbols, traditions and sporting identities. Edinburgh's festivals have made it a major international centre for theatre, comedy and literature. Southampton has a strong maritime identity and is one of the country's major passenger ports. Tea, pubs, football, cricket and fish and chips are familiar cultural shorthand, but regional differences are substantial. English has absorbed vocabulary from Celtic, Norse, French, Latin and many other languages.

name: Greece
atAGlance: Population about 10.4 million; area 131,957 km²; nominal GDP around US$280 billion; capital Athens; language Greek; currency euro (EUR). Borders Albania, North Macedonia, Bulgaria and Türkiye; the Aegean and Ionian seas connect it to Italy and the wider Mediterranean.
government: Greece is a parliamentary republic and an EU and NATO member. Its institutions are stable and electoral competition is real. Current debates include cost of living, public services, migration, regional security, transport safety and the legacy of the sovereign-debt crisis. The economy has recovered from the severe crisis of the 2010s, but public debt and demographic trends remain long-term challenges.
economy: Tourism and shipping are signature sectors, supported by food and agriculture, energy, construction, logistics, retail and professional services. Greek shipowners control a large share of the world's merchant fleet. Islands and archaeological heritage attract visitors year-round. Investment and productivity remain uneven across regions.
timeline: Minoan Crete and Mycenaean centres developed complex palace societies and trade networks in the Bronze Age. Classical Athens and other city-states influenced philosophy, drama, history, architecture and political thought in the 5th century BCE. Alexander the Great extended Macedonian power from Greece to Egypt and the borders of India. Rome incorporated Greece in 146 BCE; the eastern Roman/Byzantine Empire later centred on Constantinople. Ottoman rule continued for centuries until the Greek War of Independence (1821–1830). Greece joined the European Communities in 1981.
people: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle (philosophers); Homer (epic poet of the ancient tradition); Maria Callas (opera singer); Melina Mercouri (actor and politician); Giannis Antetokounmpo (basketball, born in Athens to Nigerian parents).
culture: Greece has thousands of islands and islets, though only a minority are permanently inhabited. The modern Olympic Games were revived in Athens in 1896. Greek cuisine centres on olive oil, vegetables, legumes, seafood, grilled meats, cheese and meze. Crete has a distinct food culture and Minoan history; Santorini's volcanic soils contribute to distinctive wines. The Greek alphabet influenced Latin and Cyrillic scripts and supplied many mathematical symbols.

name: Hong Kong
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
status: Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China — not a sovereign state.
atAGlance: Population about 7.5 million (end-2025 estimate); area 1,114 km²; nominal GDP around US$425–430 billion; capital is not separately designated (Victoria Harbour is the historic and commercial centre); official languages Chinese and English, with Cantonese most widely spoken; currency Hong Kong dollar (HKD). Borders Shenzhen in mainland China; Macau and the Pearl River Delta are nearby.
government: Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China under the “one country, two systems” framework. It has its own currency, immigration controls, courts and economic system under the Basic Law, while defence and foreign affairs are responsibilities of the central government. The 2020 National Security Law and subsequent electoral changes have materially narrowed political competition and freedoms. Commercial life remains highly developed, but political autonomy is more limited than in earlier decades.
economy: Finance, professional services, trading, logistics, aviation, retail, tourism and real estate are central. Hong Kong is an international financial centre and a gateway for investment between mainland China and global markets. Its port, airport, common-law system and convertible currency have historically been competitive advantages. High housing costs, ageing and competition from other Asian hubs are key challenges.
timeline: The Qing dynasty ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain after the First Opium War in 1842. Britain acquired southern Kowloon in 1860 and a 99-year lease of the New Territories in 1898. Japan occupied Hong Kong during World War II. Sovereignty transferred from Britain to China in 1997, when Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region. Pro-democracy movements in 2014 and 2019 highlighted disputes over electoral reform and autonomy. The 2020 national security law and later legislation reshaped its political and legal environment.
people: Bruce Lee (martial artist and actor); Jackie Chan (actor and stunt performer); Anita Mui (singer and actor); Wong Kar-wai (film-maker); Maggie Cheung (actor); Leslie Cheung (singer and actor).
culture: Hong Kong combines one of the world's best-known skylines with country parks, hiking trails, beaches and outlying islands. The Star Ferry and double-decker trams are everyday transport icons. Dim sum is traditionally a social meal of small dishes served with tea; yum cha means “drink tea.” Around three-quarters of Hong Kong's land area is not built up, much of it protected countryside. Cantonese opera, temples, colonial architecture, contemporary art and finance coexist in a compact space.

name: Honduras
atAGlance: Population about 11 million; area 112,492 km²; nominal GDP about US$40 billion; capital Tegucigalpa; language Spanish (Garifuna, Miskito and other Indigenous languages are spoken); currency Honduran lempira (HNL). Borders Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua; the Caribbean lies to the north and the Gulf of Fonseca opens to the Pacific in the south.
government: Honduras is a presidential republic with competitive elections, but its institutions face long-running challenges from corruption, organised crime, weak rule of law, poverty and political polarisation. Nasry Asfura took office on 27 January 2026 after a highly contentious 2025 election and prolonged count; rival Salvador Nasralla disputed the result. This is an important current governance issue, although the Bay Islands and Roatán's resort areas have a different day-to-day profile from some mainland regions.
economy: Agriculture (coffee, bananas, palm oil, shrimp and melons), apparel assembly, remittances, mining and services are important. Tourism is growing around the Bay Islands and archaeological sites. Remittances support household consumption, while poverty, storm exposure and limited infrastructure weigh on long-term development.
timeline: The Maya city of Copán flourished in western Honduras and became a major centre of sculpture, astronomy and writing. Columbus reached the Caribbean coast in 1502; Spain colonised the region during the 16th century. Honduras joined the Central American independence movement in 1821. The 1969 “Football War” with El Salvador was rooted in deeper migration, land and political tensions, with football matches acting as a trigger. A military-backed coup removed President Manuel Zelaya in 2009. The 2025–2026 disputed election again tested institutional resilience.
people: Berta Cáceres (environmental and Indigenous rights activist); José Cecilio del Valle (independence-era intellectual); Guillermo Anderson (musician); David Suazo and Maynor Figueroa (football).
culture: Roatán is part of the Bay Islands, alongside the Mesoamerican Reef, a globally important marine ecosystem. Copán is a UNESCO-listed Maya site famous for carved stelae and its hieroglyphic stairway. Garifuna communities have a distinctive Afro-Indigenous language, music and food culture; punta is a well-known musical expression. A popular snack is the baleada, a flour tortilla folded around refried beans and other fillings.

name: Indonesia
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
atAGlance: Population about 286 million; area 1,904,569 km²; nominal GDP around US$1.4–1.5 trillion; capital Jakarta (the national capital transition to Nusantara is a long-term project); language Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) alongside hundreds of regional languages; currency Indonesian rupiah (IDR). Land borders with Malaysia on Borneo, Papua New Guinea on New Guinea and Timor-Leste on Timor; maritime neighbours include Singapore, the Philippines and Australia.
government: Indonesia is a presidential republic and competitive electoral democracy. Concerns include political dynasties, corruption, the role of the military, pressure on civil society and concentration of executive power. A highly current development emerged on 11 November 2026: Reuters reported, citing an aide and parliamentary sources, that Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka had tendered his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and was expected to submit a formal letter to the upper house. The constitutional process still matters: the chamber must declare a vacancy before the president nominates replacements and an election is held. Treat this as breaking news and recheck before publishing an app update. [Reuters, 11 November 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/over-100-indonesian-lawmakers-sign-petition-that-could-lead-vice-presidents-2026-11-11/). The country is diverse and decentralised across thousands of islands.
economy: Consumer services, manufacturing, commodities, agriculture, mining, tourism and a fast-growing digital sector are important. Indonesia is a major producer of coal, palm oil, nickel, rubber and natural gas; nickel processing and battery supply chains have grown in strategic importance. Domestic demand is large, but infrastructure and development vary sharply across islands. Bali's tourism economy is only one part of the national picture.
timeline: Maritime kingdoms such as Srivijaya and Majapahit linked the archipelago to trade across the Indian Ocean and South China Sea. Portuguese, Dutch and other European trading posts appeared from the 16th century, and Dutch control expanded into the East Indies. Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed independence in 1945; the Netherlands transferred sovereignty in 1949 after an independence struggle. Mass killings and political violence accompanied the transition from Sukarno to Suharto in 1965–1966. The 1998 Asian Financial Crisis and protests ended Suharto's long presidency and began the Reformasi era.
people: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta (independence leaders); Pramoedya Ananta Toer (writer); Raden Saleh (painter); Anggun (singer, born in Jakarta); Liliyana Natsir (badminton champion).
culture: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic state, with more than 17,000 islands and hundreds of languages. Bali is culturally distinct because Balinese Hindu traditions shape its temples, ceremonies, art and calendar; Indonesia as a whole has the world's largest Muslim-majority population. Komodo dragons are native to a small group of islands; orangutans live in the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo. Try nasi goreng, satay, rendang, tempeh and sambal. Volcanic landscapes, coral reefs and rainforests make Indonesia exceptionally biodiverse.

name: Iceland
atAGlance: Population about 392,000; area 103,000 km²; nominal GDP around US$39 billion; capital Reykjavík; language Icelandic (English is widely understood); currency Icelandic króna (ISK). An island in the North Atlantic with no land borders; Greenland, the Faroe Islands, Norway and the UK are the nearest neighbours by sea.
government: Iceland is a parliamentary republic with a president as head of state and a prime minister responsible to parliament. It is a stable Nordic democracy with high institutional trust and strong civil liberties. Coalition governments are common. Policy discussions include housing, immigration, energy development, fisheries management and the balance between tourism and fragile ecosystems. Iceland is in NATO but has no standing army; security relies on alliances and coast-guard capabilities.
economy: Fisheries, tourism and energy-intensive industry are traditional pillars. Geothermal and hydroelectric power support aluminium smelting, data centres and other electricity-intensive businesses. Tourism is a major export earner. The small economy is exposed to global travel cycles, fish stocks, volcanic disruptions and metal prices.
timeline: Norse settlers began establishing permanent communities around 874. The Alþingi (Althing) was founded in 930 and is often described as one of the world's oldest continuing parliamentary institutions. Iceland came under the Norwegian crown in the 13th century and later the Danish crown. It became a republic in 1944. The Cod Wars with the UK (1958–1976) concerned fishing limits and maritime jurisdiction. The 2008 banking collapse caused a severe financial crisis, followed by extensive reforms.
people: Björk (singer and artist); Halldór Laxness (Nobel Prize-winning writer); Vigdís Finnbogadóttir (first woman elected president in a national election); Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval (artist); Eiður Guðjohnsen (football).
culture: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart; volcanic and geothermal activity are everyday geography. Geothermal energy heats homes and swimming pools. Northern lights are visible in dark months, while summer brings very long daylight. Icelandic sagas preserve medieval stories of exploration, family feuds and settlement. Landscapes include glaciers, black-sand beaches, waterfalls, hot springs, lava fields and active volcanoes.

name: Italy
cruiseCalls: Civitavecchia (Rome), Genoa, La Spezia, Livorno (Florence and Pisa), Naples, Messina (Sicily)
atAGlance: Population about 59 million; area 301,340 km²; nominal GDP around US$2.5–2.6 trillion; capital Rome; language Italian, with German, French, Slovene and several other regional languages recognised or protected in some areas; currency euro (EUR). Borders France, Switzerland, Austria and Slovenia, and encloses the independent states of Vatican City and San Marino.
government: Italy is a parliamentary republic and EU member. Coalition politics can be volatile, and governments face difficult budget and reform choices. Long-running issues include public debt, slow productivity growth, youth unemployment, an ageing population and the economic gap between the industrial north and the less prosperous south. The country remains a stable democracy with an independent judiciary and competitive politics.
economy: Italy is a high-income manufacturing and services economy. Machinery, vehicles, pharmaceuticals, fashion, design, food and beverages, chemicals, tourism and business services are key sectors. Family-owned small and medium-sized firms remain important. Regional specialisation is strong: northern industrial districts, central cultural tourism, and southern agriculture and tourism all contribute differently.
timeline: Rome's traditional founding date is 753 BCE; the Republic and Empire shaped law, language and engineering across the Mediterranean. The western Roman imperial government ended in 476 CE, while the Byzantine Empire continued. The Renaissance flourished in city-states such as Florence, Venice, Milan and Rome. The Kingdom of Italy unified most of the peninsula in 1861; Rome became capital in 1871. Fascist rule under Mussolini lasted from 1922 to 1943. A 1946 referendum established the Italian Republic.
people: Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo (artists); Dante Alighieri (poet); Galileo Galilei (scientist); Giuseppe Verdi (composer); Sophia Loren (actor); Enrico Fermi (physicist).
culture: Italy has 20 regions and intensely regional food traditions: Ligurian pesto, Neapolitan pizza, Roman pasta dishes, Sicilian citrus and sweets, and Tuscan breads. Roman roads, aqueducts and amphitheatres still shape the landscape. Espresso is a social ritual; ordering a cappuccino after lunch is less common in traditional cafés than an espresso. Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island and reflects Greek, Roman, Arab, Norman and Spanish influences. The country has the Alps, Apennines and active volcanoes.

name: Japan
cruiseCalls: Aomori, Hakodate, Hiroshima, Kagoshima, Kobe, Kochi, Miyazaki, Muroran, Nagasaki, Nagoya, Naha (Okinawa), Osaka, Sakaiminato, Shimizu (Mount Fuji), Toba, Tokyo (Yokohama)
atAGlance: Population about 123 million; area 377,975 km²; nominal GDP around US$4.4 trillion; capital Tokyo; language Japanese (Ainu and Ryukyuan languages are part of the country's linguistic heritage); currency Japanese yen (JPY). Japan is an island country with no land borders; maritime neighbours include Russia, the Koreas, China and Taiwan.
government: Japan is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary cabinet system; the emperor is the symbolic head of state. It is a stable democracy with competitive politics and an independent judiciary. Debates include demographic ageing, immigration, defence policy, energy security and relations with China and the Koreas. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's governing coalition secured a strong mandate in a February 2026 general election, according to the Prime Minister's Office. Japan is a key US ally and a major Indo-Pacific power.
economy: Japan combines advanced manufacturing and high-end services. Autos, machinery, robotics, electronics, precision components, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance, retail and tourism are important. Japan is a global leader in industrial automation and high-quality manufacturing. Demographic ageing, a shrinking workforce, public debt and energy-import dependence are long-term challenges.
timeline: Yayoi-era agriculture and metallurgy spread through much of the archipelago from around 300 BCE. The Tokugawa shogunate governed from Edo (Tokyo) from 1603 to 1868. US naval pressure and domestic reform movements ended the shogunate; the Meiji Restoration began rapid industrial and political transformation. Japan fought in World War II and surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and Soviet entry into the war. The 1947 constitution established parliamentary democracy and Article 9's renunciation of war. Tokyo hosted the 1964 Olympics as the first Shinkansen line opened.
people: Hokusai (artist); Akira Kurosawa (film-maker); Hayao Miyazaki (animation director); Haruki Murakami (writer); Shigeru Miyamoto (video-game designer); Yoko Ono (artist and musician).
culture: Japan comprises thousands of islands, with Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku forming the core. The Shinkansen is known for punctuality, safety and engineering. Cherry-blossom viewing, autumn foliage, summer festivals and New Year shrine visits structure the annual calendar. Food is much more varied than sushi: ramen, soba, tempura, okonomiyaki, kaiseki and regional seafood all have strong local traditions. Volcanic geography makes hot springs (onsen) a longstanding part of domestic travel and bathing culture.

name: South Korea
atAGlance: Population about 51.7 million; area 100,449 km²; nominal GDP around US$1.8–1.9 trillion; capital Seoul; language Korean, written using Hangul; currency South Korean won (KRW). South Korea shares a heavily fortified land border with North Korea; the Yellow Sea and East Sea separate it from China and Japan.
government: South Korea is a presidential republic with a directly elected president and unicameral National Assembly. It is a vibrant democracy with active media and civil society. It experienced a major constitutional crisis after former president Yoon Suk Yeol's martial-law declaration in December 2024 and subsequent impeachment; an early election in 2025 restored an elected government. Political polarisation remains, but democratic institutions demonstrated resilience. Security policy is shaped by North Korea and the US alliance.
economy: A high-income, export-oriented economy built around semiconductors, electronics, automobiles, shipbuilding, batteries, petrochemicals, steel, finance and digital services. Cultural exports—film, television, music, games and cosmetics—have become a powerful global industry. The economy is exposed to international trade and semiconductor cycles; demographic decline and youth employment are major domestic concerns.
timeline: The Three Kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla shaped the peninsula; Silla unified much of it in the 7th century. Goryeo gave Korea the name used in many languages; Joseon later ruled for more than five centuries. Japan annexed Korea in 1910; colonial rule ended with Japan's surrender in 1945. Two states emerged in 1948. The Korean War (1950–1953) devastated the peninsula; an armistice established the Demilitarised Zone but no peace treaty. Democratic reforms from 1987 established the modern competitive political system.
people: King Sejong (associated with Hangul's creation); Yi Sun-sin (naval commander); Kim Yuna (figure skating); Son Heung-min (football); Bong Joon-ho (film-maker); BTS (music group); Lee Jung-jae (actor).
culture: Hangul was created in the 15th century under King Sejong and is praised for its systematic design. Jeju has a volcanic landscape and a tradition of haenyeo—women free-divers who harvest seafood without breathing equipment. The Korean Wave (Hallyu) spans K-pop, dramas, cinema, beauty, fashion and food. Korean cuisine features kimchi, barbecue, bibimbap, stews, noodles and fermented foods. Busan is a major port and film city; Jeju is a volcanic island with a strong local identity.

name: Morocco
atAGlance: Population about 38.4 million; area 446,550 km² excluding the disputed Western Sahara territory; nominal GDP roughly US$180 billion; capital Rabat; official languages Arabic and Amazigh (French is widely used in business and education; Spanish is common in parts of the north); currency Moroccan dirham (MAD). Borders Algeria to the east and the disputed Western Sahara territory to the south; it faces Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar and Mediterranean.
government: Morocco is a constitutional monarchy. King Mohammed VI retains substantial authority over major policy and strategic sectors, while an elected parliament and government manage day-to-day administration. Multiparty elections take place, but political power is not distributed like that of a fully parliamentary monarchy. Civil liberties, protest and media expression face restrictions. Western Sahara's status remains disputed: Morocco claims sovereignty, while the United Nations lists it as a non-self-governing territory.
economy: Phosphate mining and fertiliser production are strategic sectors, alongside automotive and aerospace manufacturing, textiles, agriculture, fisheries, tourism, logistics and renewable energy. Tangier Med is a major Mediterranean-Atlantic shipping hub. Economic priorities include industrial upgrading, drought resilience, water security and reducing regional disparities. Tourism and remittances are important sources of foreign exchange.
timeline: Amazigh peoples have long inhabited North Africa; Phoenician and Roman trading settlements also developed along the coast. Idris I founded a dynasty in 789 that helped establish an early Moroccan state; Fez became a centre of learning. Almoravid and Almohad dynasties linked Morocco with much of the Maghreb and Iberia. Morocco became a French protectorate in 1912, with a Spanish protectorate in the north and south, and regained independence in 1956. The 2011 constitution followed regional protest movements but left the monarchy as the central political institution.
people: Ibn Battuta (14th-century traveller, born in Tangier); Fatima al-Fihri (traditionally credited with founding al-Qarawiyyin in Fez); Nawal El Moutawakel (Olympic champion); Tahar Ben Jelloun (writer); Achraf Hakimi (football).
culture: Morocco has both Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts; the Atlas Mountains divide coastal plains from the Sahara-facing interior. It is one of the world's leading phosphate producers. Mint tea is a symbol of hospitality; pouring it from a height aerates the tea. Argan trees are native to southwestern Morocco, and goats sometimes climb into their branches. Food combines Amazigh, Arab, Andalusian, Saharan and sub-Saharan influences: couscous, tagine, pastilla and harira are well-known examples.

name: Montenegro
atAGlance: Population about 623,000; area 13,812 km²; nominal GDP roughly US$9 billion; capital Podgorica; languages include Montenegrin, Serbian, Bosnian, Albanian and Croatian; currency euro (EUR), adopted unilaterally. Borders Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Kosovo and Albania; has a short Adriatic coastline.
government: Montenegro is a multiparty parliamentary democracy and an EU candidate country. EU accession is its central strategic project and has encouraged judicial and electoral reforms. Corruption, organised crime, polarisation, media pressures and uneven institutional capacity remain concerns. Montenegro joined NATO in 2017. The country uses the euro but is not an EU member or formal euro-area member.
economy: Tourism is a major driver, especially along the Adriatic coast and around the Bay of Kotor. Other sectors include electricity generation, metals, agriculture, construction, transport and services. The small economy imports many goods and is exposed to seasonal tourism, external investment and regional transport links.
timeline: Illyrian communities lived in the area before Roman rule; later it became part of Byzantine and Slavic political worlds. Medieval Duklja and Zeta were important regional polities. The Congress of Berlin recognised Montenegro as independent in 1878. It was incorporated into the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918 and became one of the six republics of socialist Yugoslavia after 1945. Montenegro regained independence after a 2006 referendum.
people: Petar II Petrović-Njegoš (poet, bishop and ruler); Milovan Đilas (writer and political figure); Rambo Amadeus (musician); Dejan Savićević and Stevan Jovetić (football); Marija Vuković (high jumper).
culture: The name Montenegro is usually understood as “Black Mountain,” referring to dark forested mountains. The Bay of Kotor resembles a fjord but is geologically a drowned river valley (a ria). The Tara River Canyon is among Europe's deepest river canyons. Coastal towns blend Venetian, Byzantine, Ottoman and Slavic influences.

name: Mexico
atAGlance: Population about 132 million; area 1,964,375 km²; nominal GDP around US$1.8–1.9 trillion; capital Mexico City; language Spanish, alongside 68 recognised Indigenous language groups; currency Mexican peso (MXN). Mexico borders the United States, Guatemala and Belize, with coastlines on the Pacific, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean.
government: Mexico is a federal presidential republic with 31 states and Mexico City. President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in October 2024. Elections are competitive and the public sphere is vigorous, but organised crime, impunity, corruption, attacks on journalists and controversial institutional reforms place pressure on rule of law. Conditions differ greatly between states and cities; the traveller's experience in Cozumel is not a proxy for every part of the country.
economy: Mexico is deeply integrated with the United States and Canada through the USMCA trade agreement. Important sectors include vehicles, electronics, aerospace, machinery, energy, mining, food and beverages, agriculture, finance and tourism. It is a major silver producer and vehicle exporter. Manufacturing supply chains and tourism are particularly important to the national economy.
timeline: Olmec centres flourished along the Gulf Coast; Maya, Zapotec, Mixtec and other civilizations developed sophisticated cities, calendars and trade networks. Mexica settlers founded Tenochtitlan in 1325. Spanish forces and Indigenous allies defeated the Aztec Empire in 1521, establishing New Spain. The independence struggle began in 1810 and ended in 1821. The Mexican Revolution (1910–1920) transformed land, labour and political institutions. NAFTA began in 1994 and was replaced by the USMCA in 2020.
people: Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera (artists); Octavio Paz (Nobel Prize-winning poet); Guillermo del Toro (film-maker); Carlos Santana (musician, born in Jalisco); Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (writer and intellectual of the colonial era).
culture: Corn, chocolate, vanilla, tomatoes and chillies have deep histories in Mesoamerica. Día de los Muertos is a family-centred remembrance tradition, not simply a Mexican Halloween. UNESCO recognises traditional Mexican cuisine as intangible cultural heritage. Cozumel sits beside the Mesoamerican Reef and near the Yucatán's cenotes—freshwater-filled limestone sinkholes. Regional foods include Yucatán cochinita pibil, Oaxacan mole, tacos al pastor and seafood from the coasts.

links.label: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH)

name: Malaysia
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
atAGlance: Population about 34 million; area 330,803 km²; nominal GDP around US$470 billion; capital Kuala Lumpur (administrative capital: Putrajaya); official language Malay, with English, Mandarin, Tamil and Indigenous languages widely used; currency Malaysian ringgit (MYR). Borders Thailand, Indonesia and Brunei by land; Singapore is linked by causeways and bridges; the South China Sea separates Peninsular Malaysia from Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo.
government: Malaysia is a federal constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy. The federal king is elected on a rotating basis among nine hereditary Malay rulers. The 2022 election produced a hung parliament and a broad governing coalition; the country has since had a period of relative parliamentary continuity. Coalition politics, identity-based parties, royal institutions, corruption questions and restrictions on some forms of expression complicate governance. Sabah and Sarawak have distinct political and cultural contexts.
economy: Electronics and semiconductors, electrical machinery, palm oil, oil and gas, rubber, medical devices, automobiles, food processing, tourism and financial services are major sectors. Malaysia is deeply integrated into Asian supply chains, especially electronics assembly and testing. Penang is an important manufacturing cluster; Kuala Lumpur is the services and finance centre. Commodity exports and environmental sustainability are continuing policy issues.
timeline: The Malacca Sultanate became a major trading centre linking India, China and the Malay world in the 15th century. Portuguese forces captured Malacca in 1511; Dutch and British influence followed. The Federation of Malaya was established in 1948 and independence from Britain achieved on 31 August 1957. Malaysia formed in 1963 by joining Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore; Singapore left the federation in 1965. Rapid industrialisation followed, and the 2018 election ended the long uninterrupted rule of the Barisan Nasional coalition.
people: Tunku Abdul Rahman (independence leader); P. Ramlee (actor and musician); Michelle Yeoh (actor, born in Ipoh); Jimmy Choo (shoe designer); Nicol David and Lee Chong Wei (racquet-sport champions).
culture: Malaysian culture is shaped by Malay, Chinese, Indian and Indigenous communities; food is a visible cultural meeting point. Penang is famous for hawker dishes such as char kway teow, assam laksa and nasi kandar. Borneo's Sabah and Sarawak contain rainforest and rich Indigenous cultures. The Petronas Twin Towers were once the world's tallest buildings. Durian is intensely loved by some and disliked by others—the smell is memorable.

name: Norway
cruiseCalls: Ålesund, Bergen, Haugesund, Honningsvåg (North Cape), Kristiansand, Molde, Nordfjordeid, Oslo, Skjolden, Tromsø, Trondheim
atAGlance: Population about 5.6 million; area 385,207 km² including Svalbard and Jan Mayen; nominal GDP around US$530 billion; capital Oslo; language Norwegian (Bokmål and Nynorsk written standards; Sami languages have official status in some areas); currency Norwegian krone (NOK). Borders Sweden, Finland and Russia; a long coastline faces the North Atlantic, Norwegian Sea and Barents Sea.
government: Norway is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy. It has strong rule-of-law institutions and broad social trust. Policy debates include energy transition, oil and gas production, regional services, immigration, Arctic security and the management of fisheries and natural resources. Norway is a NATO member but not an EU member; it participates in the European Economic Area and Schengen arrangements.
economy: Oil and gas are major export earners, complemented by shipping, seafood, hydropower, metals, manufacturing, financial services and tourism. The Government Pension Fund Global invests petroleum revenues internationally and is among the world's largest sovereign wealth funds. High incomes and an extensive welfare state are supported by natural resources, productivity and a relatively small population.
timeline: The Viking Age (c. 800–1050) connected Norway to trade, exploration and settlement across the North Atlantic. Norway entered the Kalmar Union in 1397 and later remained in political union with Denmark. It adopted a constitution in 1814 before entering a union with Sweden. The union was peacefully dissolved in 1905. Nazi Germany occupied Norway in 1940–1945. North Sea oil discoveries from 1969 onward transformed the economy and public finances.
people: Edvard Munch (artist); Henrik Ibsen (playwright); Edvard Grieg (composer); Roald Amundsen (polar explorer); Sonja Henie (figure skater); Magnus Carlsen (chess grandmaster).
culture: Fjords are glacially carved inlets; steep walls and deep waters shaped settlement and transport. North of the Arctic Circle, summer brings midnight sun and winter offers aurora viewing. Brown cheese (brunost) is made by slowly heating whey until its sugars caramelise. Coastal express ships and ferries are lifelines as well as tourist transport. Friluftsliv expresses a broad appreciation of outdoor life.

name: Puerto Rico
status: Unincorporated, organised US territory with commonwealth status — not a US state and not an independent country.
atAGlance: Population about 3.2 million; area 8,870 km²; nominal GDP around US$125–130 billion; capital San Juan; official languages Spanish and English (Spanish is most widely used in daily life); currency US dollar (USD). It lies east of the Dominican Republic and west of the US Virgin Islands.
freedom: Not covered as a separate territory.
government: Residents are US citizens and elect a governor and local legislature. Puerto Rico elects a resident commissioner to the US House of Representatives, who does not have a final floor vote. Residents of the island do not vote in the US presidential general election while living there. Congress retains ultimate authority under the US Constitution. Political debate includes statehood, independence and continuation or reform of the current territorial relationship. Jenniffer González-Colón has served as governor since January 2025. A separate Freedom House country score is not published.
economy: Pharmaceuticals, medical devices, chemicals and other manufacturing are important, alongside tourism, finance, trade and government-related activity. US legal and commercial links shape investment and trade. Debt restructuring, hurricane recovery, electricity-grid reliability, population decline and cost of living remain major issues.
timeline: Taíno communities inhabited the island, which they called Borikén/Borinquen. Columbus reached Puerto Rico in 1493 and Spanish rule followed. Spain ceded the island to the United States after the Spanish-American War in 1898. The Jones–Shafroth Act granted US citizenship to Puerto Ricans in 1917. A commonwealth constitution took effect in 1952, creating locally elected self-government within the US territorial framework. Debt restructuring, migration and repeated status referenda have kept the island's future relationship with the US in public debate.
people: Roberto Clemente (baseball legend and humanitarian); Rita Moreno (actor and EGOT winner); José Ferrer (actor); Lin-Manuel Miranda (writer and composer); Bad Bunny (musician); Julia de Burgos (poet).
culture: The coquí, a tiny tree frog with a distinctive call, is a beloved cultural symbol. Puerto Rico has several bioluminescent bays, where microorganisms create a blue-green glow in the water. Salsa, reggaeton and Latin trap have strong Puerto Rican roots and influence. Local food blends Taíno, African and Spanish influences: try mofongo, arroz con gandules, pasteles and local coffee. El Yunque is the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System.

name: Portugal
atAGlance: Population about 10.8 million; area 92,090 km² including Madeira and the Azores; nominal GDP around US$345 billion; capital Lisbon; language Portuguese (Mirandese has protected status); currency euro (EUR). Borders Spain to the east and north; Atlantic Ocean to the west and south. Madeira and the Azores are autonomous island regions.
government: Portugal is a semi-presidential republic with a directly elected president and an elected parliament; the prime minister leads the government. Coalition bargaining and the rise of smaller parties have made politics more fragmented, but democratic institutions remain well established. Major policy debates include housing affordability, wages, health services, migration, productivity and the balance between tourism and residents' needs. Portugal has been an EU member since 1986.
economy: Services, tourism, trade, finance, logistics, technology and public administration are major contributors. Manufacturing remains important in vehicles, machinery, footwear, textiles, cork, paper and food products. Portugal is a leading cork producer and has expanded renewable electricity, especially wind and solar. Madeira and the Azores have island economies centred on tourism, agriculture, fisheries and public services.
timeline: The Treaty of Zamora recognised Portugal as a kingdom in 1143; the mainland borders have been unusually stable for centuries. Portuguese forces captured Ceuta in 1415, a milestone in maritime expansion. In the 15th and 16th centuries Portuguese navigators established trading routes to Africa, India, Southeast Asia and Brazil. The 1755 Lisbon earthquake, tsunami and fires devastated the capital, prompting major reconstruction. A revolution overthrew the monarchy in 1910. The Carnation Revolution ended the Estado Novo dictatorship in 1974; Portugal joined the European Communities in 1986.
people: Vasco da Gama (navigator); Fernando Pessoa (poet); Amália Rodrigues (fado singer); José Saramago (Nobel Prize-winning writer); Cristiano Ronaldo (football); Paula Rego (artist).
culture: Azulejos—painted ceramic tiles—decorate churches, stations, palaces and ordinary homes and form a visual record of history. Madeira is associated with fortified wine and dramatic levada walks; the Azores are volcanic islands with crater lakes, hot springs and whale-watching grounds. Fado is a soulful song tradition associated especially with Lisbon and Coimbra. Portuguese custard tarts (pastéis de nata) are famous worldwide.

name: Sweden
atAGlance: Population about 10.6 million; area 450,295 km²; nominal GDP around US$670 billion; capital Stockholm; language Swedish, with Finnish, Meänkieli, Sami, Romani and Yiddish having national minority-language status; currency Swedish krona (SEK). Borders Norway and Finland; the Baltic Sea separates Sweden from Denmark, Germany, Poland and the Baltic states.
government: Sweden is a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy with high civil liberties. The September 2026 election produced a hung parliament: the incumbent bloc lost its majority, while the opposition has struggled to assemble the votes required to govern. On 10 November, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was given another week to try to form a government. This is a coalition-formation impasse within established constitutional procedures, not a collapse of democratic institutions. Policy debates include migration and integration, crime prevention, energy supply, regional inequality, welfare services and defence. Sweden joined NATO in 2024 and the EU in 1995. [Reuters, 10 November 2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/swedish-pm-kristersson-given-another-week-try-form-new-government-2026-11-10/).
economy: Advanced manufacturing, vehicles, telecoms, pharmaceuticals, machinery, mining, forestry, paper, financial services and creative industries are key sectors. Sweden has globally recognised industrial companies and a strong innovation ecosystem. Its economy is export-oriented and closely connected to Europe and global markets.
timeline: Swedish-linked Norse traders travelled east through the Baltic and river routes during the Viking Age. Sweden entered the Kalmar Union in 1397. Gustav Vasa became king in 1523 and Sweden emerged as an independent kingdom. Sweden lost Finland to Russia in 1809. The union with Norway was peacefully dissolved in 1905. Sweden joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
people: Alfred Nobel (inventor and founder of the Nobel Prizes); Astrid Lindgren (writer); Selma Lagerlöf (Nobel Prize-winning writer); ABBA (pop group); Ingmar Bergman (film-maker); Zlatan Ibrahimović (football).
culture: Fika is a Swedish social coffee break, often accompanied by cinnamon buns. Visby on Gotland preserves a remarkable medieval walled town and reflects the island's role in Hanseatic trade. Sweden's creative exports include pop music, video games, crime fiction, design and fashion. Daylight hours vary dramatically between summer and winter. Food traditions include pickled herring, crispbread, berries and seasonal dishes.

name: Singapore
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
atAGlance: Population about 6.1 million; area about 735 km²; nominal GDP around US$600 billion; capital Singapore; official languages English, Malay, Mandarin Chinese and Tamil (English is the main language of government and business); currency Singapore dollar (SGD). Singapore is a city-state at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, linked to Malaysia by causeways and separated from Indonesia by narrow straits.
government: Singapore is a parliamentary republic; a president is head of state and the prime minister leads government. Public institutions are highly capable and predictable, with a strong business rule-of-law reputation. Political competition, public protest and media space are more constrained than in liberal democracies. The People's Action Party has governed continuously since independence. The country is administratively stable, while civil-liberties and opposition-space debates remain important.
economy: Finance, global trade, port and airport logistics, pharmaceuticals, biomedical science, semiconductors, petrochemicals, professional services and technology are major sectors. Its strategic location and high-quality infrastructure make it a major international business and shipping hub. The economy depends heavily on global trade and imported food, energy and labour.
timeline: Stamford Raffles established a British trading post in 1819, and Singapore became a Crown Colony in 1867. Japan occupied the island during World War II; its fall in 1942 was a major shock to the British Empire. Singapore gained self-government in 1959 and joined the Federation of Malaysia in 1963. It separated from Malaysia and became an independent republic in 1965. Rapid industrialisation, education and housing investment transformed the city-state.
people: Lee Kuan Yew (founding prime minister); S. Rajaratnam (diplomat and founding leader); Joseph Schooling (Olympic swimmer); Tan Swie Hian (artist and poet); JJ Lin (singer and songwriter); Catherine Lim (writer).
culture: Singapore is a city-state: the country and its principal city are effectively the same place. Hawker centres are a defining part of daily food culture; Singapore's hawker culture is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. The port and airport are major logistics hubs. Gardens by the Bay and extensive street greenery express the ambition to combine dense urban development with nature. The local word “can” means “yes, it can be done” and is a recognisable feature of Singlish.

name: Turks and Caicos Islands
status: British Overseas Territory — not an independent country.
atAGlance: Population about 47,000; area 948 km²; nominal GDP approximately US$1.7–1.8 billion (latest comparable data may be older than the 2026 political snapshot); capital Cockburn Town; language English; currency US dollar (USD). The island group lies southeast of the Bahamas and north of Hispaniola.
government: The territory has an elected House of Assembly and a local government led by a premier, alongside a UK-appointed governor. The Progressive National Party formed the government after the 7 February 2025 general election; Charles Washington Misick is premier. The UK retains responsibility for defence and external affairs and holds reserved constitutional powers. A standalone Freedom House country score is not published for the territory.
economy: Tourism, luxury accommodation, real estate, construction, financial services and fisheries are the main pillars. The US dollar is used, and the economy is closely tied to North American visitors and investment. The small domestic market imports much of its food and fuel; hurricanes, coastal erosion, water supply and pressure on infrastructure are important long-term concerns.
timeline: Lucayan Taíno communities lived in the islands before European arrival. Grand Turk and Salt Cay became known for salt production and export in the 17th and 18th centuries. The islands were administered with the Bahamas, then with Jamaica from 1874 to 1959. After Jamaica's independence, they became a separate British colony and later a British Overseas Territory under evolving self-government arrangements.
culture: The islands' public history is closely tied to salt, seafaring and later tourism. Grand Turk is known for its historic salt ponds, colonial-era buildings, clear water and nearby coral reefs. The name “Turks” is often linked to the Turk's-cap cactus; “Caicos” is commonly traced to a Lucayan term referring to a chain of islands. Conch appears in fritters, salad and chowder. Flamingos and marine ecosystems are part of the archipelago's natural identity.
