name: Thailand
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
atAGlance: Population about 71.6 million; area 513,120 km²; nominal GDP around US$575–580 billion; capital Bangkok; language Thai; currency Thai baht (THB). Borders Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia; the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Sea connect it to the region.
government: Thailand is a constitutional monarchy with a parliamentary system, but military and judicial institutions have had outsized influence in modern politics. Elections have repeatedly been followed by coups, court rulings, party dissolutions and constraints on speech about the monarchy. Anutin Charnvirakul was appointed prime minister for a second term in March 2026 after the February election; a Constitutional Court challenge to that election was dismissed in September. The government has a large coalition, but structural political tensions remain.
economy: Tourism, automotive manufacturing, electronics, food processing, healthcare, agriculture, rice, rubber, petrochemicals and logistics are important. Thailand is a regional manufacturing hub and a long-established tourism destination. Household debt, ageing, inequality and productivity growth are recurring concerns.
timeline: Sukhothai emerged as an early Thai kingdom in the 13th century; Ayutthaya later became a major regional power. Burmese forces destroyed Ayutthaya in 1767; a new kingdom was established at Thonburi and then Bangkok. The Chakri dynasty began in 1782. A 1932 revolution ended absolute monarchy and introduced constitutional government. Siam avoided formal colonisation by a European power, though it ceded territory and navigated pressure from Britain and France. The country adopted the name Thailand in 1939.
people: King Bhumibol Adulyadej (long-reigning monarch); Tony Jaa (actor and martial artist); Apichatpong Weerasethakul (film-maker); Lisa/Lalisa Manobal (musician); Buakaw Banchamek (Muay Thai fighter).
culture: Songkran, the Thai New Year festival in April, is famous for water celebrations but also has religious and family traditions. Theravada Buddhism shapes temples, festivals and daily life. Thai cuisine balances sour, sweet, salty, spicy and bitter flavours; regional dishes include northern khao soi, Isan som tam and southern curries. Phuket has a strong Chinese-Thai heritage alongside its beaches; its old town preserves colourful Sino-Portuguese architecture.

name: Türkiye
atAGlance: Population about 86 million; area 783,562 km²; nominal GDP roughly US$1.6 trillion; capital Ankara; language Turkish (Kurdish, Arabic and other languages are also used); currency Turkish lira (TRY). Borders Greece and Bulgaria in Europe, and Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan (Nakhchivan), Iran, Iraq and Syria in Asia.
government: Türkiye is an executive presidential republic and NATO member, with substantial authority concentrated in the presidency. It has formal multiparty elections, but major concerns persist about judicial independence, opposition rights, media freedom and the treatment of critics. The European Commission's 2026 assessment describes continuing rule-of-law backsliding. Inflation, currency volatility, refugee policy, relations with the EU and regional security are central issues. “Türkiye” is the country's official preferred English name in formal writing; “Turkey” remains common in English.
economy: A large, diversified economy spans manufacturing, automobiles, textiles, appliances, construction, tourism, agriculture, food processing, defence industries, logistics and financial services. It is a bridge between European and Asian supply chains. High inflation and currency depreciation have complicated household budgets and investment planning, while tourism and manufacturing earn foreign exchange.
timeline: The Hittite Empire was a major Anatolian power in the second millennium BCE. Emperor Constantine made Byzantium an imperial capital in 330 CE; Constantinople became the centre of the eastern Roman/Byzantine state. Ottoman forces captured the city in 1453. The Ottoman Empire collapsed after World War I; the Turkish War of Independence led to the republic. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk proclaimed the Republic of Türkiye in 1923 and pursued sweeping secular and modernising reforms.
people: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (founder of the republic); Orhan Pamuk (Nobel Prize-winning novelist); Nâzım Hikmet (poet); Aziz Sancar (Nobel Prize-winning scientist); Ara Güler (photographer); Tarkan (pop musician).
culture: Istanbul spans two continents, divided by the Bosporus. Ephesus was one of the great cities of the ancient Mediterranean; its nearby Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Turkish coffee is finely ground and simmered, with grounds settling in the cup. Turkish food ranges from Aegean olive-oil dishes to southeastern kebabs, Black Sea anchovies and pistachio desserts of Gaziantep.

name: Taiwan
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
status: Self-governing multiparty democracy; its international status is disputed.
atAGlance: Population about 23.3 million (end-2025 official household-registration count); area 36,197 km²; nominal GDP about US$920 billion (2025 estimate); capital Taipei; Mandarin is most widely used, alongside Taiwanese Hokkien, Hakka and Indigenous languages; currency New Taiwan dollar (TWD). No land borders; the Taiwan Strait separates it from mainland China, with Japan to the northeast and the Philippines to the south.
government: Taiwan is self-governing: its elected government controls its territory, armed forces and domestic institutions. The People's Republic of China claims Taiwan as part of its territory, while Taiwan's international diplomatic recognition is limited and its status contested. Taiwan has a competitive multiparty democracy and extensive civil liberties. Cross-strait relations remain a major security issue; the region's strategic importance makes the issue highly visible in international diplomacy. Explain its status neutrally rather than reducing it to a simple “country” label.
economy: Taiwan is a high-income, export-oriented economy whose strategic industries include semiconductors, electronics, precision machinery, information technology, petrochemicals, finance and advanced manufacturing. It is central to global chip supply chains, particularly foundry manufacturing. Exports, especially semiconductor-related trade, are major economic drivers. Energy imports, demographic ageing and cross-strait uncertainty are key challenges.
timeline: Dutch forces established a foothold in southwest Taiwan from 1624; the Zheng family displaced them in 1662. Taiwan was incorporated into the Qing Empire in 1683. Japan governed Taiwan from 1895 to 1945. The Republic of China took control after Japan's surrender; after the Chinese civil war, the ROC government relocated to Taiwan in 1949. Martial law and one-party rule constrained politics until 1987. Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996 and developed into a competitive democracy.
people: Lee Teng-hui and Tsai Ing-wen (former presidents); Ang Lee (film director); Teresa Teng (singer); Jay Chou (musician); Audrey Tang (digital-policy innovator); Yani Tseng (golfer).
culture: Taiwan is a world centre for advanced semiconductor manufacturing; chips inside phones, cars and data centres often have a Taiwan connection. Night markets are a major part of urban culture, with oyster omelettes, beef noodle soup, stinky tofu and bubble tea. Bubble tea emerged in Taiwan in the 1980s and became a global phenomenon. The island is mountainous, with peaks above 3,000 metres, hot springs and subtropical forests. Indigenous peoples have Austronesian languages and cultures linking Taiwan to a much wider Pacific history.

name: United States
atAGlance: Population about 342 million; area about 9.83 million km² total; nominal GDP roughly US$30–31 trillion; capital Washington, DC; no federal official language (English is dominant and Spanish is widely spoken); currency US dollar (USD). Land borders are with Canada and Mexico; nearby maritime neighbours include the Bahamas, Cuba and Russia across the Bering Strait.
government: The United States is a federal constitutional republic with 50 states and a presidential system. It retains competitive elections, constitutional protections and an independent judiciary, while political polarisation and strain on institutional oversight are significant themes in recent democracy assessments. Federalism means rules, taxes and public services can differ substantially by state. Florida's political and legal environment is not identical to that of other states.
economy: The world's largest nominal economy combines finance, technology, healthcare, professional services, retail, manufacturing, energy, aerospace, entertainment, agriculture and logistics. The dollar and US capital markets have global influence. Florida tourism and aerospace around Cape Canaveral are only small windows into a very diverse national economy.
timeline: Hundreds of distinct Indigenous nations and cultures lived across the continent before European colonisation. The Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1776; the Constitution followed in 1787. The Civil War (1861–1865) ended slavery and preserved the Union, while leaving a long legacy of racial inequality. The 19th Amendment (1920) prohibited denying the vote on the basis of sex. The civil-rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s dismantled legal segregation and expanded voting protections. Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon in 1969; Kennedy Space Center near Port Canaveral remains a major spaceflight site.
people: George Washington and Abraham Lincoln (presidents); Martin Luther King Jr. (civil-rights leader); Katherine Johnson (mathematician); Maya Angelou (writer); Duke Ellington, Aretha Franklin and Beyoncé (music); Walt Disney (animation and entertainment).
culture: The country has 63 national parks plus a much larger protected-land system. Florida is a meeting point of Caribbean, Latin American and mainland US influences; the Everglades is a vast subtropical wetland ecosystem. Port Canaveral is close to Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Food, accents, music and customs vary dramatically from state to state: “American culture” is not one uniform thing.

name: Vietnam
region: Southeast Asia and East Asia gateways
cruiseCalls: Chân Mây (Da Nang gateway), Phu My (Ho Chi Minh City gateway)
atAGlance: Population about 101.6 million; area 331,212 km²; nominal GDP around US$515 billion; capital Hanoi; language Vietnamese; currency Vietnamese đồng (VND). Borders China to the north and Laos and Cambodia to the west; the South China Sea/East Sea lies to the east and south.
government: Vietnam is a one-party socialist republic led by the Communist Party of Vietnam. It has stable one-party governance and long-term policy continuity, but no competitive national multiparty elections and significant restrictions on political opposition, independent media and public dissent. Leadership transitions take place within the Communist Party. “Political stability” in the sense of institutional continuity should not be confused with political freedom.
economy: Vietnam is a major manufacturing and export hub, producing electronics, phones, apparel, footwear, furniture, machinery and processed foods. Agriculture remains important, including rice, coffee, seafood and tropical fruit. Tourism, logistics, retail and financial services are growing. The National Statistics Office estimated 2025 GDP at approximately US$515 billion, with manufacturing and services leading output.
timeline: Vietnamese forces won independence from Chinese rule under Ngô Quyền in 939, beginning a long history of self-governing dynasties. The Nguyễn dynasty unified the country in 1802 and established an imperial capital at Huế. French conquest began in the 1850s and Vietnam became part of French Indochina. Hồ Chí Minh declared independence in 1945; war followed against France. The 1954 French defeat at Điện Biên Phủ and Geneva Accords divided Vietnam temporarily. Saigon fell in 1975, reunification followed in 1976, and the Đổi Mới market reforms began in 1986.
people: Hồ Chí Minh (revolutionary leader); Nguyễn Du (poet); Võ Nguyên Giáp (military commander); Trịnh Công Sơn (songwriter); Bao Ninh (writer); Đặng Thái Sơn (pianist).
culture: Vietnam has 54 officially recognised ethnic groups and distinct regional food traditions. Coffee culture is distinctive: robusta beans, drip filters, condensed milk and egg coffee are all part of the story. Phở is internationally famous, but regional versions differ; central Vietnamese food often features more chilli and complex sauces. Water puppetry developed in the Red River Delta. Tết, the Lunar New Year, is the most important annual holiday and a major time for family reunions.
